concepts.label: Inner products, norms and orthogonality
concepts.note: course background (not a lecture); placed first in lecture order

concepts.label: Constrained optimisation: Lagrangian, KKT, quadratic programming
Kernel trick (kernel functions, polynomial and RBF kernels, validity)

edge_audit.rater1_note: the margin is a distance computed with w^T x / ||w||
edge_audit.codex_reason: Mastering geometric margin requires understanding inner products, normal-vector norms and orthogonal distance to a hyperplane.

edge_audit.rater1_note: the margin is defined for a linear separator h(x)=sign(w^T x + b)
edge_audit.codex_reason: A student can master hyperplane margin through geometry without mastering perceptron learning, PLA or linear regression.
Mastering hard-margin SVM requires understanding the margin that its optimization objective maximizes.

edge_audit.rater1_note: the dual and the support vectors need KKT; but a student can know the primal SVM as a QP without Lagrange multipliers
edge_audit.codex_reason: Mastering the hard-margin primal, dual and support-vector characterization requires the core Lagrangian, KKT and quadratic-programming concepts.

edge_audit.rater1_note: CS 156 teaches the kernel trick through the SVM dual; kernels exist outside SVMs, so a student can know kernels without SVMs
edge_audit.codex_reason: Although standard SVM instruction introduces kernels through the hard-margin dual, kernels can be mastered through other methods such as kernel ridge regression.

edge_audit.rater1_note: a kernel is an inner product in a transformed Z space
edge_audit.codex_reason: Mastering the kernel trick requires understanding its interpretation as inner products in an implicitly transformed feature space.

edge_audit.rater1_note: K(x,x') = z^T z' is an inner product
edge_audit.codex_reason: Mastering kernels and their validity requires understanding the inner-product geometry that a valid kernel represents.

edge_audit.rater1_note: soft margin relaxes the hard-margin constraints with slack
edge_audit.codex_reason: A student can master slack variables and C through a direct soft-margin formulation without mastering the hard-margin dual and support-vector characterization.

edge_audit.rater1_note: the transform makes a linear model in Z space
edge_audit.codex_reason: Nonlinear feature mappings can be mastered without mastering the linear-model learning algorithms that typically motivate their introduction.

edge_audit.rater1_note: Lecture 14 motivates the margin with VC/dichotomy arguments (instructional), but a student can know and use the SVM without knowing VC dimension
edge_audit.codex_reason: VC dimension can motivate generalization discussions but is unnecessary for learning or mastering the hard-margin SVM formulation.

edge_audit.rater1_note: the course derives d_VC of the perceptron; VC dimension as a notion does not need linear models
edge_audit.codex_reason: Linear classifiers commonly introduce shattering examples, but VC dimension can be mastered using other hypothesis classes without learning linear-model algorithms.

edge_audit.rater1_note: found by the non-edge audit (recall sample)
edge_audit.codex_reason: Mastering linear models including linear regression requires the inner-product and orthogonality concepts underlying predictions and least-squares residuals.

non_edges.codex_reason: Kernel functions, implicit feature maps and kernel validity can be mastered without VC-dimension theory.
Lagrangian optimization supports the SVM application of kernels but is unnecessary for teaching or mastering the kernel trick itself.
Slack variables and C can be taught and mastered entirely for linear soft-margin SVMs in the original input space.
Mastering linear models including linear regression requires the inner-product and orthogonality concepts underlying predictions and least-squares residuals.
Constrained optimization typically precedes the soft-margin derivation, but slack and C can be mastered through their geometric and loss interpretations.
Inner-product geometry is standard preparation, but algebraic mastery of Lagrangians, KKT conditions and quadratic programs need not imply mastery of norms and orthogonality.
VC dimension concerns shattering by hypothesis classes and can be taught and mastered without nonlinear feature transformations.
Margin is relevant to kernelized SVMs but is unnecessary for teaching or mastering kernels as implicit feature-space inner products.

audit_summary.note: Agreement is model-vs-model, never human agreement. All edges need_human_review until the author or mentor rates them.

items.text: For u = (1, 2, -1) and v = (3, 0, 2), what is the inner product u^T v?
Vectors u and v satisfy ||u|| = 3, ||v|| = 4 and u^T v = 0. What is ||u + v||?
Let w be a nonzero vector in R^d. Which statement about the set P = {x : w^T x = 0} is true?

choices.b: w is orthogonal to every vector in P.
choices.c: P contains only the zero vector.
choices.d: P is a sphere of radius ||w||.
choices.e: Scaling w by 2 changes the set P.

items.rationale: For x in P, w^T x = 0, which is the definition of orthogonality; scaling w does not change P.

items.text: For u = (3, 4), what is the largest value of u^T x over all unit vectors x (||x|| = 1)?
items.rationale: By Cauchy-Schwarz u^T x <= ||u|| ||x|| = 5, reached at x = u/||u||.

items.text: A perceptron in R^2 has weights w = (w0, w1, w2) = (-1, 2, 1), where w0 is the bias weight. What does it output for the input x1 = 0.2, x2 = 0.3?

choices.e: It depends on the learning rate.

items.text: The perceptron learning algorithm (PLA) picks a misclassified point (x, y), with y in {-1, +1}. What is its weight update?

choices.b: w <- w + y x

items.rationale: PLA adds y x; option e is the least-mean-squares (Adaline) update, not PLA.

items.text: For linear regression with data matrix X (N x (d+1)) and targets y, with X^T X invertible, which weight vector minimises the in-sample squared error?

choices.b: (X^T X)^{-1} X^T y

items.rationale: The normal equations X^T X w = X^T y give the pseudo-inverse solution.

items.text: If a training set is linearly separable, what does the perceptron learning algorithm do?

choices.b: It stops after a finite number of updates with a separating w.
choices.c: It always returns the maximum-margin separator.
choices.d: It converges only if the learning rate decays to zero.
choices.e: It stops only if N < d + 1.

items.rationale: The perceptron convergence theorem: finite updates on separable data; the result is some separator, not the maximum-margin one.

items.text: A linear classifier is trained in Z space with the transform Phi(x1, x2) = (1, x1^2, x2^2). What kind of decision boundary can it give in the original X space?

choices.b: Conics centred at the origin with axes along x1 and x2 (for example circles, ellipses, hyperbolas).
choices.e: A boundary that cannot be drawn in X space.

items.rationale: w0 + w1 x1^2 + w2 x2^2 = 0 is an axis-aligned conic centred at the origin.

items.text: The full second-order polynomial transform of x = (x1, x2) includes the constant 1. How many coordinates does z have?
items.rationale: z = (1, x1, x2, x1^2, x1 x2, x2^2): 6 coordinates.

items.text: Why is a very high-dimensional nonlinear transform risky for generalisation?

choices.a: It always makes the in-sample error larger.
choices.b: The VC dimension of the linear model in Z grows with the dimension of Z, so the generalisation bound gets looser.
choices.c: It removes the ability to fit the training data.
choices.e: It has no effect on generalisation.

items.rationale: A linear model in Z of dimension d~ has d_VC = d~ + 1.

items.text: Points with x1^2 + x2^2 < 1 are labelled +1 and points with x1^2 + x2^2 > 1 are labelled -1 (no point lies exactly on the circle). Which transform makes the data linearly separable?

choices.e: No transform can make it separable.

items.rationale: In z = (1, r^2) the threshold r^2 = 1 separates the classes.

items.text: Which is the definition of the VC dimension d_VC of a hypothesis set H with growth function m_H(N)?

choices.b: The largest N with m_H(N) = 2^N.
choices.c: The number of parameters of H.
choices.e: The N at which the training error reaches zero.

items.rationale: Option a is the break point k; d_VC = k - 1.

items.text: What is the VC dimension of the perceptron in R^d (with a bias weight)?

choices.b: d

items.rationale: d_VC of the d-dimensional perceptron is d + 1.

items.text: What is the VC dimension of positive rays on the real line, h(x) = sign(x - a)?
items.rationale: One point can be shattered; two points cannot (the left +1, right -1 labelling is impossible).

items.text: If a hypothesis set has a finite VC dimension, what does VC theory guarantee?

choices.b: With enough data, E_out is close to E_in with high probability.

items.rationale: The VC bound makes E_out - E_in small with high probability as N grows.

items.text: Minimise f(x) = x^2 subject to x >= 1, with the Lagrangian L(x, a) = x^2 - a (x - 1) and a >= 0. What are the optimal x and multiplier a?
items.rationale: The constraint is active at x = 1; dL/dx = 2x - a = 0 gives a = 2.

items.text: In the KKT conditions for inequality constraints, what does complementary slackness say about a multiplier a_n?

choices.b: a_n can be positive only if the n-th constraint holds with equality.
choices.c: a_n = 0 means the n-th constraint is violated.
choices.e: The multipliers do not depend on the constraints.

items.rationale: a_n * (slack of constraint n) = 0.

items.text: Which problem is a quadratic programming (QP) problem?

choices.a: A quadratic objective with quadratic constraints.
choices.b: A linear objective with quadratic constraints.
choices.c: A quadratic objective with linear equality and inequality constraints.
choices.d: Any convex objective with any constraints.
choices.e: A quadratic objective over integer variables.

items.rationale: QP = quadratic objective, linear constraints (b is a linear program).

items.text: What is the distance from the point x = (3, 4) to the hyperplane w^T x + b = 0 with w = (3, 4) and b = -5?
A separating hyperplane (b, w) is scaled so that min_n |w^T x_n + b| = 1. What is the distance from the hyperplane to the nearest training point?
items.rationale: The distance of x_n is |w^T x_n + b| / ||w||, which is 1/||w|| for the nearest point.

items.text: Why prefer a separating line with a large margin over one with a small margin?

choices.a: It always has lower in-sample error.
choices.b: Fat separators can implement fewer dichotomies, which acts like a smaller effective VC dimension and tends to generalise better.
choices.c: It is the only separator that exists.
choices.d: It is always faster to compute.
choices.e: There is no reason; all separators are equal.

items.rationale: All separators have E_in = 0; the large margin restricts the hypothesis set.

items.text: In the hard-margin SVM solution, which training points are the support vectors?

choices.b: Points with a_n > 0; they lie on the margin boundary.
choices.d: The points farthest from the hyperplane.

items.rationale: Support vectors have positive dual variables and satisfy y_n (w^T x_n + b) = 1.

items.text: In the dual of the hard-margin SVM, how is the optimal weight vector w obtained from the dual variables a_n?

choices.b: w = sum_n a_n y_n x_n

items.rationale: Setting the gradient of the Lagrangian with respect to w to zero gives w = sum a_n y_n x_n.

items.text: You remove a training point that is not a support vector and retrain the hard-margin SVM. What happens?

choices.b: The solution stays the same.

items.rationale: The solution depends only on the support vectors.

items.text: Which quantity gives an upper bound on the leave-one-out cross-validation error of the hard-margin SVM trained on N points?

choices.b: d / N, where d is the input dimension

items.rationale: Removing a non-support vector leaves the solution unchanged, so only support vectors can be leave-one-out errors.

items.text: A kernel computes K(x, x') = z^T z' with z = Phi(x). What does the kernel trick let an SVM do?

choices.a: Work in Z space without computing z, because the dual and the final hypothesis need only inner products.
choices.b: Avoid quadratic programming.
choices.c: Reduce the VC dimension to zero.

items.rationale: The dual objective and g(x) use z only through inner products, which K supplies.

items.text: What is the dimension of the feature space Z that matches the Gaussian (RBF) kernel K(x, x') = exp(-gamma ||x - x'||^2) with gamma > 0 on R^d?
items.rationale: The Gaussian kernel matches an infinite-dimensional transform.

items.text: Which condition makes a function K(x, x') a valid kernel (Mercer's condition)?

choices.a: Any function of two vectors is a valid kernel.
choices.b: K is symmetric and its Gram matrix is positive semi-definite for every set of points.
choices.d: K must be linear in x.

items.rationale: Mercer: symmetric with positive semi-definite Gram matrices.

items.text: In the soft-margin SVM, what does a larger value of the parameter C do?

choices.a: It penalises margin violations more; on separable data the solution approaches the hard-margin SVM as C grows.
choices.b: It allows more margin violations.
choices.c: It sets the width of the kernel.
choices.e: It fixes the number of support vectors directly.

items.rationale: C weights the total slack in the objective.

items.text: In the soft-margin SVM, a training point has slack xi_n = 1.5 at the optimum. Which statement is true?

choices.a: It is correctly classified and outside the margin.
choices.b: It is inside the margin but correctly classified.
choices.d: It is not a support vector.
choices.e: It lies exactly on the margin boundary.

items.rationale: y_n (w^T x_n + b) = 1 - 1.5 = -0.5 < 0, so the point is on the wrong side.

items.text: How does the dual of the soft-margin SVM differ from the dual of the hard-margin SVM?

choices.b: Each dual variable gets an upper bound: 0 <= a_n <= C.

items.rationale: The slack variables add the box constraint 0 <= a_n <= C.
